# Sounding lead, rutters and coastal pilotage (`sounding_lead_pilotage`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/navigation.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Navigation, transport & exploration (`navigation`)
- Deps: helped by dead_reckoning_log_line, map_projection_charts, tides_tide_tables
- Core idea: Near land the depth and the kind of bottom tell where you are: a lead weight on a line marked in fathoms (about 1.8 m) is thrown ahead, and a hollow in its base filled with tallow brings up sand, shell, mud or gravel to compare with the written sailing directions (rutters, routiers, periploi), which list depths, bottoms, landmarks, courses and tides harbour by harbour. Sound continuously at night and in fog when approaching a coast, and anchor when the depth shoals unexpectedly.
- Pitfalls:
  - Relying on deep-sea lines near cliffs; many coasts drop straight to great depth, so no bottom does not mean safety
  - Trusting a rutter from another season or tide state
  - Dismissing pilotage as primitive; in the North Sea and Channel it was the main method well into the 18th c.
- History: greece: 5th c. BC – Herodotus reports sounding a day's sail off Egypt (11 fathoms, mud); europe: c. 1250–1296 – Compasso da navigare (Mediterranean rutter); 15th c. Low German Seebuch; written 1483–84 Pierre Garcie's routier for Atlantic coasts; islamic: c. 1490 – Ibn Majid's rahmani (rutters) for the Indian Ocean; china: 15th–16th c. – Shunfeng xiangsong rutter of compass courses
- Read:
  - Herodotus, Histories II.5
  - David W. Waters, The Rutters of the Sea: The Sailing Directions of Pierre Garcie (1967)
